newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FOCUS-S.Africa Telkom gets $1bln privatisation boost.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-S.Africa Telkom gets $1bln privatisation boost.

text.p: South Africa's Telkom will get a $1 billion cash injection following its partial privatisation, paving the way for a massive roll-out of new phone lines, Deputy President Thabo Mbeki said on Tuesday.

The sale of the 30 percent stake of the state telecommunications concern, the largest privatisation deal in Sub-Saharan Africa and the first major sell-off in South Africa, is expected to net around $1.3 billion, according to industry analysts.
The balance of the proceeds will go to the state, Mbeki told a telecommunications conference.

"Government has decided on the injection of $1 billion of the proceeds of the sale into Telkom to help fund the infrastructure expansion programme. The rest of the proceeds will go to the National Revenue Fund," he said.
"This will commit Telkom to one of the most aggressive roll-out programmes of its kind in the world."
Mbeki said government had approved the finalisation of the sale of the Telkom stake to a consortium comprising SBC Communications Inc and Telekom Malaysia Bhd.
Signing of the deal is expected within days. "Negotiations are taking place as we speak to finalise the detailed legal agreements that underpin this agreement," Mbeki said.
Telkom's strategic equity partners would make a one-off payment in dollars at the close of the deal, which could be one week to 90 days from the signing, officials said.
Some 50,000 jobs are expected to be created in the telecommunications sector alone from increased capital expenditure at Telkom which will almost double in the next five years.
"The boost to the economy will be enormous," Mbeki said.
Foreign exchange dealers said the injection of well over $1 billion into the economy would help the rand and bolster foreign exchange reserves which currently stand at around $2.8 billion.
The use of the balance of the proceeds to cut government debt could also help government bonds, although some economists had hoped that a larger proportion of receipts would go direct to the state.

For Telkom, the landmark deal will provide badly-needed capital, expertise and technology to enable it to overcome the legacy of the apartheid era which has left millions of mainly black South Africans without access to a telephone.
Telephone penetration in South Africa's affluent and mainly white suburbs is typically around 80 percent. But in the neighbouring townships the rate can fall to under three percent.
Mbeki said Telkom would target certain priority customers in in its new line roll-out programme, including 24,000 schools, hospitals, libraries and villages.
SBC and Telekom Malaysia both see great scope for growing the telecommunications market in southern Africa, a region in which both have already made commitments.

SBC already has a presence in South Africa through its 15 percent stake in the cellular phone operator MTN while Telekom Malaysia, which was itself privatised in 1990, is backing the South Africa Far East cable project.
